content.text: This unit has covered many aspects of magnetism and electromagnetism. From permanent magnets to transformers, from motors to generators, the same fundamental principles connect everything. This lesson summarises the key concepts, shows how they relate to each other, and provides practice in applying them together.

The entire magnetism unit rests on two fundamental effects: the motor effect (current + field = force) and the generator effect (changing flux = induced voltage). Motors, generators, transformers, speakers, and microphones all rely on one or both of these principles.
Current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.
Changing magnetic flux through a conductor induces a voltage.
Induced current opposes the change causing it.
Motors and generators are essentially the same device
A motor running backwards is a generator
A generator running backwards is a motor
Same applies to microphones and loudspeakers

When faced with an unfamiliar exam question about electromagnetic devices, first identify which effect is at work. If a current is given and you need to find a force, it is the motor effect (F = BIL, left-hand rule). If motion or changing flux is given and you need to find a voltage, it is the generator effect (right-hand rule, Faraday's Law).
Motor uses electromagnetic principles for continuous rotation
All rely on changing magnetic flux inducing voltage
Generator: mechanical rotation provides the change
Transformer: AC current provides the change
Generators produce AC at power stations
Transformers step up voltage for transmission
Transformers step down for safe use
Is there current and field given?
Is there motion and field given?
Is there AC and coils mentioned?
Check direction using hand rule if needed
A wire of length 0.2 m carries a current of 5 A perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
This is the motor effect (current in field → force).
A coil with 100 turns rotates in a magnetic field. The flux through the coil changes by 0.05 Wb in 0.25 s. Calculate the average induced EMF.
This is electromagnetic induction (changing flux → voltage).
A transformer has 500 primary turns and 25 secondary turns. The input is 240 V AC. Calculate the output voltage.
Explain why a moving-coil loudspeaker uses the motor effect and a dynamic microphone uses the generator effect.
Coil is in magnetic field of permanent magnet
Motor effect produces force on coil
Coil moves, attached cone vibrates, producing sound
Sound waves cause diaphragm to vibrate
Attached coil moves in magnetic field
Changing flux induces voltage in coil
Electrical signal output represents the sound
Confusing left and right hand rules
Reversing current or field reverses force/voltage direction
Convert mm to m, kV to V, etc.
Remember current squared—doubling current quadruples losses

The key equations for this unit are: F = BIL (motor effect), the transformer equation Vp/Vs = np/ns, and power conservation VpIp = VsIs. Make sure you can rearrange each of these and apply them in different contexts.
Calculate the force on a wire 0.5 m long carrying 3 A in a 0.2 T field.
Calculate the induced EMF in a coil of 200 turns that experiences a flux change of 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s.
Calculate the output voltage of a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of 20:1 and an input of 400 V.
Explain why transformers only work with AC, referring to electromagnetic induction.
Calculate the frequency of the output when a generator coil rotates at 1500 rpm.
Describe the energy transfers in: a) A DC motor b) An AC generator
Calculate the following for 100 MW of power transmitted through cables of resistance 2 ohm at 500 kV: a) The current b) The power loss
Changing magnetic fields create electric fields
Lenz's law ensures no free energy
— Direct substitution into the motor effect formula. (calculation)
EMF = n x (change in flux / time) = 200 x (0.02 / 0.1) = 200 x 0.2 = 40 V
— Apply Faraday's law with n turns. (calculation)
— A 20:1 step-down transformer divides the voltage by 20. (calculation)

Transformers rely on a changing magnetic field in the core to induce a voltage in the secondary coil. AC continuously changes direction, producing a continuously changing flux. DC produces a constant current and therefore a constant magnetic field — with no change in flux, no voltage is induced in the secondary coil.
— Convert revolutions per minute to revolutions per second. (calculation)
DC motor: electrical energy (from the supply) is transferred to kinetic energy (rotation) plus thermal energy (wasted in coil resistance, friction, and eddy currents) and sound energy.
AC generator: kinetic energy (from the turbine/rotation) is transferred to electrical energy plus thermal energy (wasted in coil resistance and friction) and sound energy.
P_loss = I²R = 200² x 2 = 80 000 W = 80 kW = 0.08 MW
— Only 0.08% of the transmitted power is lost. (calculation)
